rationale: B wins because it catches the operational and proof traps instead of decorating them. Its line, "whether the chain charges a non-dairy surcharge — 'no price change at retail' covers grocery shelves, not café menus," is exactly the kind of ugly little detail that saves a pitch from dying in the first reply. A's strongest angle steps on the rake with "customers who don't specify get oat milk," turning "default non-dairy option" into a broader dairy-displacement claim the update does not support. B still overreaches with "Plant-based dairy's growth era is over," but it is more disciplined where it matters.
gaps_in_A: "customers who don't specify get oat milk" is the worst miss. The update says default non-dairy option, not default milk for every unspecified order.
"falling volumes, shrinking retail shelf space, canceled expansions" imports category context that was not in the update. Useful if proven, sloppy if assumed.
The set leans on "no price change at retail" but misses the cafe-pricing question. Retail shelf price does not answer whether the 1,400-location chain charges a non-dairy surcharge.
"surviving brands are choosing depth over breadth" turns one company's cost cut plus one distribution win into a sector thesis before the required category data exists.
gaps_in_B: "Plant-based dairy's growth era is over" is too grand for the supplied facts. The caveat helps, but the headline still writes a check the evidence has not cashed.
"when an unprofitable company starts closing plants, sustainability spend is the first casualty" is asserted as a prevailing belief without proof. Frame it as the question, not the premise.
"customer-story" is only viable once the chain is named and on record. B asks for that proof, but the angle should stay conditional until then.
